title: Getting a real cert when Let's Encrypt can't reach you
summary: Why two working domains suddenly stopped renewing, why the fix wasn't the router, and what DNS-01 actually buys you over http-01.
body:
Two domains behind a Caddy instance -- both with certificates that had worked fine for months -- suddenly stopped renewing. The obvious suspects all checked out clean: router port-forwards were correct, Windows Firewall had the right allow rules, DNS resolved to the right public IP. Every piece of local diagnosis said everything was fine.

The actual evidence only showed up once Caddy's own log output was captured properly (its logging wrapper had never had stdout/stderr wired to a file -- an easy thing to skip, and it meant there had been zero visibility into why issuance was failing, for who knows how long). Once the logs were readable, the real error was blunt:

"98.127.222.7: Fetching http://<domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/...: Timeout during connect (likely firewall problem)"

That IP is Let's Encrypt's own validator -- not a router misconfig, not a Windows Firewall rule, not anything fixable from inside the machine running Caddy. Something upstream of the router was dropping inbound connections specifically from that validator's IP range on port 80, and the same thing happened on port 443 for the tls-alpn-01 fallback. Real browser traffic to the same domains worked fine -- this wasn't a blanket block, just one that happened to catch exactly the traffic ACME validation depends on.

Repeated failures compounded the problem: Let's Encrypt's own "too many failed authorizations" rate limit kicked in on top of the original issue, meaning even fixing the root cause wouldn't have produced an immediate result -- the account needed to cool down first.

The fix that actually worked: switch to a DNS-01 challenge instead. Caddy proves domain ownership by pushing a TXT record to DuckDNS's API -- a normal outbound HTTPS call -- instead of needing Let's Encrypt's validator to reach an inbound port at all. No router change, no ISP call, no firewall rule. Once the DNS-01 automation policy was in place (via the caddy-dns/duckdns plugin) and a couple of unrelated gotchas were cleared -- a stale self-signed cert whose SAN list happened to already cover the target domain, which made Caddy think it didn't need a new one at all, and an invalid .local contact email that Let's Encrypt was rejecting outright -- the real certificate issued cleanly.

Everything from that fix is now written up as a proper skill (caddy-dns-duck), specifically so the next domain that hits this doesn't need to be re-diagnosed from zero.
